result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Athens, describing temples and statues of Apollo, Aphrodite and Hercules, then the Lyceum, the tomb of Nisus and the Ilissus river. He ends with the white marble stadium built by Herodes.

scenes.title: Temple of Delphian Apollo, Theseus
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the Apollo statue and temple, and tells how Theseus, mocked by the roof builders, threw their oxen's waggon over the roof.

scenes.title: Gardens, Aphrodite and Cynosarges
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Gardens, the statue of Aphrodite by Alcamenes, and the Cynosarges with its altars to Hercules, Hebe, Alcmene and Iolaus.

scenes.title: The Lyceum
scenes.summary: The Lyceum is named for Lycus son of Pandion and is a temple of Apollo Lyceus.

scenes.title: Tomb and Story of Nisus
scenes.summary: Pausanias tells of Nisus's tomb and how his daughter cut his purple lock when Minos besieged Nisæa.
scenes.stakes: Nisus will die if his purple hair is cut off.

scenes.title: The Ilissus and Eridanus
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the rivers of Attica, Orithyia's abduction by the North Wind, the Muses' altar and Codrus's death place.

scenes.title: Agræ and the Stadium
scenes.summary: Across the Ilissus lie the temple of Artemis Agrotera and the marble stadium built by Herodes.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Aphrodite, here called oldest of the Fates.
Apollo's cult title at the Lyceum.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable anecdote of Theseus's strength answering mockery.

analysis.text: The passage shows Pausanias weaving cult sites, local legends and monuments together, tying places to heroes and myths.
The marble stadium of Herodes (Atticus) reflects second-century AD Athenian civic benefaction under Roman rule.

legacy.text: The Panathenaic Stadium built by Herodes was restored and used for the first modern Olympic Games in 1896.

fun_facts.text: The Cynosarges later became a gymnasium associated with Antisthenes and the Cynic philosophers.

language_notes.text: "Incognito" means unrecognized, with his identity concealed; Theseus was returning to Athens, where his father Ægeus was king.
"No account given" means the Athenians offered no explanation of these sites; Pausanias reports only what he can see and what he is told.
Pausanias refers to an oracle about a white dog snatching part of a sacrifice, which explained the place's name; he does not retell it here.
Nisus's purple lock was the token of his life; cutting it meant his death and the fall of his city.
The Celtic Eridanus is a distant northern river of legend, sometimes identified with the Po; only the name is shared.
"Crescent-shaped" describes the stadium's curved, horseshoe-like outline along the hillside.

context_notes.text: The feat shows Theseus's great strength and prefigures his hero's role; the builders' mockery is answered by action rather than words.
Alcamenes was a famous Athenian sculptor of the fifth century BC, a pupil of Phidias.
Lyceus is an epithet of Apollo; the Lyceum later became famous as the place where Aristotle taught.
Herodes is Herodes Atticus, a wealthy Athenian benefactor of the second century AD; Pentelican marble came from Mount Pentelicus.

literary_notes.text: The builders mock the disguised hero as a helpless maiden, unaware he is Theseus, so their jeer sets up their humiliation.
The legend gives the river a divine connection: the North Wind's marriage explains the aid he gave Athens against Persian ships.
Pausanias speaks as a traveller, contrasting what is hard to believe with what is wonderful to see and inviting the reader to share his awe.
